sentences.text: Daliansaurus was a small, lightly built troodontid dinosaur that likely possessed feathers and measured roughly one meter in length.
This genus contains only one species, Daliansaurus liaoningensis, which was formally named in 2017.
Its skull measured 13.8 centimeters long and featured four front teeth in the upper jaw that were D-shaped instead of recurved.
The animal is best recognized by a large claw on its fourth toe, a feature that makes it unique among troodontids which typically have sickle claws only on the second toe.
Daliansaurus appears to be the first troodontid known to possess a bird-like uncinate process on its ribs.
The preserved fossil shows the head and neck curled backward, the tail curved forward, and the arms positioned asymmetrically.
The remains were found in Early Cretaceous volcanic deposits dating to approximately 126 million years ago in the village of Lujiatun, Liaoning, China.
The holotype specimen, cataloged as DNHM D2885, was described in a 2017 paper by Shen Caizhi and colleagues.
This single specimen is nearly complete and preserved in three dimensions.
Histological analysis of growth lines in the radius suggests the individual was at least four years old when it died, likely having reached skeletal maturity at the size of the holotype.
Its long metatarsals likely provided superior running abilities compared to other members of the troodontid family.
Uncinate processes on the ribs may have reinforced the rib cage and improved breathing efficiency, similar to structures found in modern birds and other dinosaurs like Velociraptor.
The lower jaw had a straight margin rather than a convex one, and the animal possessed at least 21 upper and 24 lower dental alveoli, fewer than the 27 found in Sinovenator.
Teeth toward the back of the mouth in Daliansaurus have small striations on their posterior edges, a trait shared with Sinovenator.
Daliansaurus belongs to the Troodontidae family, a group of paravian dinosaurs known for sickle claws on the second toe.
It is part of the subgroup Sinovenatorinae, which also includes Mei, Sinovenator, and Sinusonasus, though the defining trait of this group is not present in Daliansaurus.
This dinosaur lived during the Barremian to Aptian stages, from 125.77 to 119.57 million years ago, in the volcanically influenced, cold climate of the Lujiatun Beds.

It is debated whether sinovenatorines like Daliansaurus coexisted strictly or replaced each other over time or were segregated by geography and ecology, as some anatomical differences may be due to individual or ontogenetic variation rather than distinct species.
